summary: A 1976 interim revision of Appendix F of BBN Report 1822, the document describing the interface between hosts and IMPs. It is a short update to that appendix.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a small correction page for the manual explaining how computers plug into the network's routers.

subtitle: Clarification of Very Distant Host interface operations

tldr.problem: Confusion existed about how to operate a host connected to an IMP (Interface Message Processor) through a Very Distant Host (VDH) interface. The host-to-IMP interface definition needed clarification about message ordering and retransmission strategy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 716 updates Appendix F of BBN Report 1822 to clarify that messages between the RTP (Remote Transmission Protocol) layers can arrive out of order, even when the host-to-IMP interface delivers in order. It recommends a 100-millisecond delay before retransmitting an unacknowledged packet and notes that immediate retransmission is possible if a later packet has been acknowledged.
tldr.outcome: This interim revision addressed operational confusion until the full report was revised. The clarification improved understanding of VDH interface behavior.

today: RFC 716 is an interim clarification published in May 1976. It addressed operational issues with the Very Distant Host interface until a full revision of BBN Report 1822 could be released.

sections.title: Very Distant Host Interface Clarification
sections.content:
RFC 716 is an interim update to Appendix F of BBN Report 1822, the specification for host-IMP interconnection. The confusion concerned how a Very Distant Host (VDH) interface—used when a host is far from its IMP—delivers messages. While a standard host-to-IMP interface delivers messages in order and receives them in order, a VDH interface can deliver from the IMP to its RTP in order, but between the two RTP layers (software interfaces) nothing guarantees ordering.

If a VDH's receiving RTP detects an error in a packet and discards it, the next packet may arrive on another channel before the sending RTP retransmits the lost one. The receiving RTP must accept this out-of-order behavior. The transmit RTP fills channels in sequence; the receive RTP empties them in sequence, ensuring overall consistency.
sections.plainLanguage: When messages hop through a special long-distance connection, they can arrive out of order between the two software layers, even though the basic connection is orderly. You have to be ready for that.

sections.title: Retransmission and Acknowledgment Strategy
sections.content:
When a packet must be retransmitted until acknowledged, processing and transmission delays can cause acknowledgement to lag by more than one transmission time. The RFC recommends that RTPs implement a programmable delay (trial value of 100 milliseconds) before retransmitting an unacknowledged packet. This prevents unnecessary retransmissions from interfering with new transmissions and reduces load on both receiver and transmitter.

An optimization is noted: if the RTP observes that a later packet has been acknowledged while an earlier one has not, it is clear that the first packet was not correctly received and can be retransmitted immediately without waiting for the programmed delay to expire. However, this optimization had not yet been implemented in the IMP at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send a message and do not hear back, wait 100 milliseconds before trying again. But if a later message gets an answer and this one does not, you can try right away because you know this one got lost.

sections.title: Application to VDH Operations
sections.content: These principles apply specifically to Very Distant Host operations where long delays and special channel handling are involved. The RFC updates the original BBN Report 1822 to document this behavior, providing clarity for implementers and operators. The out-of-order delivery at the RTP level is tolerated provided that the transmit and receive sides maintain their own sequencing discipline.
sections.plainLanguage: These rules help when your computer is far from the router. As long as both sides keep their own order, messages can hop around and still work.
